concepts.name: Article 22: Dual Structure — Ordinary Arrest vs. Preventive Detention
key_dimensions: Article 22(1)&(2) govern ordinary/punitive arrest; Article 22(3)–(7) govern preventive detention — the two operate in separate legal universes
UPSC trap: Article 22(1)&(2) protections do NOT apply to persons arrested under preventive detention laws [Article 22(3)(b)]
Distinction between punitive detention (post-offence, tried in court) and preventive detention (pre-offence, no trial)
Comparison with Article 21 (right to life) — preventive detention must satisfy both Article 21 and Article 22 safeguards simultaneously

concepts.name: Rights of Arrested Persons Under Article 22(1) and 22(2)
key_dimensions: Three mandatory rights: (i) right to be informed of grounds of arrest, (ii) right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of one's choice, (iii) right to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours
UPSC trap: The 24-hour rule excludes travel time from place of arrest to magistrate's court
After 24 hours, detention only on magistrate's authority — not police authority
Judicial interpretation: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) — elaborated procedural safeguards beyond Article 22, making them enforceable under Article 21

concepts.name: Exceptions to Article 22(1) and 22(2) Protections — Article 22(3)
key_dimensions: Two categories excluded: (a) enemy aliens, (b) persons arrested under any preventive detention law
UPSC trap: Enemy aliens are denied BOTH sets of protections — neither ordinary arrest rights nor preventive detention safeguards apply to them as a matter of right
Significance: Creates a constitutionally sanctioned 'rights-free' zone for enemy aliens — debated in scholarship
Distinction: A foreign national who is NOT an enemy alien retains Article 22(1)&(2) rights

concepts.name: Maximum Period of Preventive Detention Without Advisory Board Reference — Article 22(4) and 22(5)
key_dimensions: A person cannot be detained for more than 3 months under preventive detention unless an Advisory Board reports sufficient cause before expiry of 3 months
UPSC trap: The 3-month limit is the default ceiling for detention WITHOUT Advisory Board opinion; Parliament can prescribe a longer period WITH Advisory Board
Parliament can also prescribe detention beyond 3 months without Advisory Board reference for specified classes of cases under Article 22(7) — a major constitutional exception
44th Amendment (1978) sought to reduce the period to 2 months but was never brought into force — the 3-month rule still operates

concepts.name: Advisory Board: Composition, Role, and Constitutional Significance
key_dimensions: Must consist of persons who are, or have been, or are qualified to be appointed as, High Court judges — ensures quasi-judicial character
UPSC trap: Advisory Board is NOT a court; its opinion is advisory and the government is not legally bound to accept it, but deviation requires strong justification (judicially read)
Board must report within 7 weeks of detention (as prescribed under NSPA rules) — procedural timeline traps in MCQs
Judicial review of Advisory Board proceedings: Courts can examine whether the Board was properly constituted and followed procedure, but cannot substitute its opinion on sufficiency of cause

concepts.name: Grounds of Detention: Communication and Non-Disclosure — Article 22(5) and 22(6)
key_dimensions: Article 22(5): Detaining authority MUST communicate grounds of detention 'as soon as may be' — not necessarily immediately, but at the earliest practicable moment
Article 22(6): Authority MAY refuse to disclose facts considered against public interest — a constitutional right of non-disclosure (not a discretionary administrative act)

UPSC trap: Non-disclosure under 22(6) does not negate the obligation to communicate grounds under 22(5); the two operate simultaneously — grounds must be communicated, but specific sensitive facts may be withheld
Judicial interpretation: Grounds must be sufficient to enable detenu to make an effective representation — vague or irrelevant grounds vitiate detention (Haradhan Saha v. State of WB)

concepts.name: Right to Make Representation — Article 22(5): Scope and Judicial Expansion
key_dimensions: Article 22(5) confers the right to make a representation against the detention order to the detaining authority
Judicial expansion: Representation must be considered at the earliest opportunity — undue delay in disposing of representation vitiates continued detention
UPSC trap: Right to make representation to Advisory Board and to detaining authority are separate rights — failure to afford either independently vitiates detention
Contrast with ordinary criminal procedure: No right to legal representation before the Advisory Board is explicitly guaranteed under Article 22 — though some statutes provide it

concepts.name: Parliament's Power to Prescribe Detention Beyond 3 Months — Article 22(7): The Legislative Override
key_dimensions: Article 22(7) empowers Parliament (not State Legislature) to prescribe by law: (a) circumstances under which detention beyond 3 months without Advisory Board is permissible, and (b) maximum period of detention
UPSC trap: Only Parliament (Union Legislature) can invoke Article 22(7) — State Legislatures cannot prescribe detention beyond 3 months without Advisory Board reference
This is a major exception to the Advisory Board safeguard — often described as a potential tool for executive overreach
No such law has yet been enacted by Parliament using Article 22(7) in its full scope — a constitutionally dormant but exam-relevant provision

concepts.name: Legislative Competence Over Preventive Detention: Union vs. State
key_dimensions: Preventive detention for reasons connected with Defence, Foreign Affairs, and Security of India — Union List (Entry 9)
Preventive detention for reasons connected with security of State, maintenance of public order, maintenance of essential services — Concurrent List (Entry 3)
UPSC trap: Both Parliament AND State Legislatures can make preventive detention laws, but for different subjects; Article 22(7) override is exclusive to Parliament
Key statutes: MISA (repealed), NSA 1980 (Central), COFEPOSA 1974 (Central), Goonda Acts (State) — classification of laws to their constitutional entry is a frequent MCQ area

concepts.name: National Security Act (NSA), 1980: Provisions and Safeguards
key_dimensions: Allows detention for up to 12 months (3 months initially, extendable) for security of India, public order, or maintenance of essential services
UPSC trap: Under NSA, detention can be ordered by District Magistrate / Commissioner of Police without prior approval, but Central/State government must be informed within 12 days and can revoke
Advisory Board must confirm detention within 7 weeks for continuation beyond 3 months
Grounds must be communicated within 5 days (extendable to 10–15 days in exceptional circumstances) — this procedural detail is frequently tested

concepts.name: Preventive Detention and Article 21: The Intersection Post-Maneka Gandhi
key_dimensions: Post-Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): Procedure established by law under Article 21 must be fair, just, and reasonable — this standard applies to preventive detention laws too
A preventive detention law cannot survive if it violates Article 14 (arbitrary) or Article 19 (unreasonable restriction) — triple test from Maneka

UPSC trap: Before Maneka, preventive detention laws were largely insulated from Article 19 challenge (A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras, 1950 held each Article operates independently); Maneka overruled this isolation principle
Practical implication: Courts now examine whether the detention law and its application satisfy due process broadly, not just Article 22's narrow procedural safeguards

concepts.name: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950): The Foundation Case and Its Overruling
key_dimensions: First major SC case on preventive detention — upheld the Preventive Detention Act 1950; held that fundamental rights operate independently (silo theory)
Court held: If detention satisfies Article 22, courts cannot additionally scrutinize it under Articles 19 or 21
UPSC trap: Gopalan was effectively overruled by Maneka Gandhi (1978) on the question of inter-relationship of fundamental rights — a classic before/after comparison question

Historical significance: Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act (prohibiting disclosure of grounds) was struck down even in Gopalan — establishing that courts can strike down specific provisions of detention laws

concepts.name: Doctrine of Sufficient Cause and Subjective Satisfaction in Preventive Detention
key_dimensions: Detention order is based on 'subjective satisfaction' of the detaining authority — courts cannot substitute their opinion on whether detention was necessary

UPSC trap: Subjective satisfaction does NOT mean unreviewable — courts examine: (a) whether authority applied its mind, (b) whether grounds are relevant and not vague, (c) whether there was non-application of mind or mala fides
Judicial review is on the reasonableness of the grounds and procedural compliance, not on the merits of the detention decision
Stale or proximate cause doctrine: If grounds are based on events too remote in time from the detention order, the causal link is broken and detention is vitiated

concepts.name: Procedural Safeguards as Substantive Rights: Consequences of Non-Compliance
key_dimensions: Any failure to comply with Article 22 safeguards (e.g., non-communication of grounds, delay in referral to Advisory Board, failure to consider representation) renders detention VOID, not merely voidable
UPSC trap: Even technical procedural violations — such as communicating grounds in a language the detenu does not understand — vitiate the detention order
Habeas corpus under Article 32 / Article 226 is the primary remedy — and courts will order immediate release for procedural non-compliance
Sunita Devi v. State of Bihar: Reinforced that procedural safeguards in Article 22 are not mere formalities but substantive constitutional rights

concepts.name: Preventive Detention During National Emergency — Articles 358 and 359 Interface
key_dimensions: During National Emergency (Article 352): Article 19 rights can be suspended (Article 358) — removes one layer of challenge to detention laws
Article 359: President can suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of fundamental rights (except Articles 20 and 21)
UPSC trap: Even during Emergency, Article 22 procedural safeguards technically remain unless specifically suspended — but Article 21 enforcement may be barred, weakening judicial oversight

ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976) — held that Article 21 was the sole repository of right to life and its suspension during Emergency meant no challenge to detention; overruled by K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) which held Articles 20 and 21 are always enforceable

concepts.name: Preventive Detention Laws and Article 19 Freedoms: Constitutional Validity Tests
key_dimensions: Post-Maneka: A preventive detention law must not impose unreasonable restrictions on Article 19 freedoms — e.g., a law detaining persons for merely exercising free speech would violate Article 19(1)(a) read with 19(2)
Article 22 does not IMMUNIZE detention laws from Article 19 challenge — it merely prescribes the minimum procedure; constitutionality is separately tested under Article 19
UPSC trap: Article 22 is not a self-contained code (overruling Gopalan's silo theory) — it must be read with Articles 14, 19, and 21
COFEPOSA (Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act) upheld as valid restriction on Article 19(1)(g) — economic security rationale

concepts.name: Detenu's Right to Legal Representation Before Advisory Board
key_dimensions: Article 22 does NOT explicitly guarantee the right to be represented by a lawyer before the Advisory Board

UPSC trap: Supreme Court in A.K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) held that the detenu does NOT have an absolute constitutional right to legal representation before the Advisory Board — the law can allow or disallow it
Distinction: Right to consult a lawyer under Article 22(1) applies at the time of arrest (for ordinary arrest), not before Advisory Board
Some statutes (e.g., COFEPOSA) permit legal representation before the Advisory Board — making it a statutory, not constitutional, right in those cases

concepts.name: Successive Detention Orders: Constitutional Permissibility and Judicial Scrutiny
key_dimensions: A fresh detention order can be issued after a previous order is quashed — successive detention is constitutionally permissible if fresh grounds exist
UPSC trap: If fresh grounds are merely a reiteration of old grounds declared invalid, the fresh order will also be struck down (res judicata-like principle in detention law)
Rationale: The executive cannot circumvent judicial orders by recycling invalid grounds in new detention orders
Haradhan Saha principle: Each detention order must stand on its own independent grounds — a critical anti-circumvention safeguard

concepts.name: Preventive Detention and Bail: The 'No Bail as of Right' Principle
key_dimensions: Unlike punitive/ordinary detention, there is NO constitutional right to bail under preventive detention — the entire purpose is to detain without trial
UPSC trap: Courts cannot grant bail on merits in preventive detention cases the way they do in criminal cases — relief is through habeas corpus, not bail applications
However, courts can release detenu if detention order is procedurally or substantively invalid — functionally similar outcome but legally distinct mechanism

Comparison: In ordinary arrests under CrPC/BNSS, bail is a statutory/constitutional entitlement; in preventive detention, release comes only through successful habeas corpus or revocation by the detaining authority

concepts.name: UAPA, POTA, TADA: Special Detention Regimes and Their Constitutional Tensions
key_dimensions: TADA (repealed 1995) and POTA (repealed 2004) allowed extended detention (up to 180 days) with modified Advisory Board procedures — tested the outer limits of Article 22(7)
UAPA 2019 amendments: Allows designation of individuals as terrorists + extended custody periods — raises Article 22 and Article 21 tensions

UPSC trap: These special laws are justified under Entry 1 (Defence) or Entry 9 (Union List) and Entry 3 (Concurrent List) — not under Article 22(7) directly, but must still comply with Article 22 minimum safeguards

Judicial response: SC in Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab (1994) upheld TADA's extended detention but read down certain provisions — illustrating that even special laws are not beyond Article 22 review
